Name: self_invented_reasoning_dialect
Title: Do LLMs Need Natural Language to Reason, or Can They Invent a Better One? Bootstrapping and Testing Self-Constructed Symbolic Dialects
Short Hypothesis: LLMs can be induced to invent a compact, self-consistent symbolic 'reasoning dialect' (a private notation system with its own tokens/grammar) that departs from natural language, and reasoning in this self-invented dialect can match or exceed natural-language chain-of-thought while being more token-efficient and less parasitic on natural-language priors. This tests whether the communicative grammar of natural language is essential to LLM reasoning, or whether language merely provides a reusable serial symbolic substrate that a model can re-design for itself.
Related Work: Prior work spans: (1) CoT (Wei et al.) and concise-reasoning self-training (Munkhbat et al. 2025) which compress natural-language traces but keep them natural-language; (2) latent/continuous reasoning (COCONUT, Hao et al.) which removes language entirely into vectors; (3) filler-token studies (Pfau et al., Lanham et al.) showing content-free tokens partially substitute for reasoning; (4) neuralese/emergent-communication literature where agents evolve codes for a channel. None examine whether a single pretrained LLM can DELIBERATELY DESIGN its own explicit, human-inspectable symbolic notation for reasoning and whether that notation preserves reasoning quality and transfers across problems/models. Unlike latent reasoning (opaque vectors) our dialect stays in the discrete token space and is legible; unlike filler tokens it carries real structured information; unlike concise-CoT it is not constrained to natural language grammar. This directly probes the language↔intelligence question: is natural language a necessary scaffold or a re-designable convenience?
Abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning is almost always expressed in natural language, leaving open whether the grammar and lexicon of human language are essential to LLM reasoning or merely a convenient serial substrate. We ask whether an LLM can invent its OWN reasoning language—a compact symbolic dialect with self-defined tokens and conventions—and reason in it as well as, or better than, in English. We propose a three-stage protocol. First, INVENT: through iterative self-play on a training task distribution, a model proposes and refines a private notation (a legend mapping recurrent reasoning moves to short symbols) selected to minimize trace length while preserving correctness under self-verification. Second, USE: the model solves held-out problems using only its invented dialect, and we compare accuracy and token efficiency against natural-language CoT, concise-CoT, and filler-token baselines. Third, TEST necessity: we causally corrupt the dialect's legend, shuffle symbol meanings, and transplant one model's dialect into another model to measure whether the dialect encodes genuine reusable structure or merely leans on residual natural-language priors. We evaluate open models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2) on arithmetic, algorithmic, logical, and multi-hop tasks. We hypothesize that self-invented dialects (i) match natural-language CoT accuracy while using substantially fewer tokens, (ii) degrade sharply under legend corruption (showing the symbols carry real information, unlike filler), and (iii) transfer partially across models, revealing shared latent reasoning structure. Results would clarify whether natural language is necessary for LLM intelligence or a re-designable interface, with implications for efficient reasoning, interpretability, and language–thought coupling in AI.
Experiments: 1) TASK SUITE: assemble 4 reasoning families with automatic verifiers—multi-digit arithmetic (GSM8K-style), synthetic algorithmic/state-tracking, propositional/syllogistic logic, and 2-hop factual chains—each split into a dialect-invention training pool and a held-out test set. 2) DIALECT INVENTION LOOP: For each model (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B) run iterative self-play: (a) model proposes a 'legend' (a small table mapping recurrent reasoning operations/objects to short invented symbols) plus reasoning conventions; (b) model solves training problems using the legend; (c) accept legend revisions that reduce mean trace token length while keeping verifier-checked accuracy above a threshold (best-of-N selection, ~5–10 iterations). Freeze the final legend per task per model. 3) MAIN COMPARISON: on held-out problems, compare four trace regimes at matched inference budget—(i) natural-language CoT, (ii) self-invented dialect (legend provided in-context), (iii) concise-CoT (self-generated compressed NL), (iv) matched-length filler tokens. Metrics: final-answer accuracy, thinking-token count, accuracy-per-token efficiency. 4) NECESSITY / INFORMATION-CONTENT TESTS: (a) LEGEND-CORRUPTION—randomly remap symbol meanings in the provided legend and re-run; predict large accuracy drop for dialect (symbols carry info) but near-zero effect for filler baseline; (b) LEGEND-ABLATION—remove the legend entirely, forcing the model to interpret its own symbols without the mapping; (c) SEMANTIC-SHUFFLE—keep symbols but scramble their assignments to operations. 5) CROSS-MODEL TRANSFER: take model A's invented legend and force model B to reason with it; measure accuracy vs B's own dialect and vs random-symbol control; quantify a 'shared-structure' transfer score. 6) LEGIBILITY / STRUCTURE ANALYSIS: measure legend properties—symbol reuse rate, compression ratio vs NL, whether invented symbols align with known operators—and correlate these with accuracy. 7) SCALING & GENERALIZATION: test whether a dialect invented on one task family transfers to another (cross-task generalization). METRICS: accuracy, tokens/trace, accuracy-per-token, corruption-induced accuracy drop (Δ), cross-model transfer score, compression ratio; all with mixed-effects models (random effects for problem and model) and effect sizes.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Models may fail to invent stable useful notations and default to disguised English; we detect this via the legend-corruption test (if corruption doesn't hurt, the dialect isn't doing real work) and report it as an informative outcome. 2) Tokenizer effects: invented symbols may tokenize inefficiently, confounding token-efficiency claims; we report token counts and choose tokenizer-friendly symbols where possible. 3) The invention loop's acceptance criterion could overfit to training problems; we always evaluate on held-out sets and cross-task transfer. 4) In-context legend inclusion adds prompt tokens; we account for this in total-budget accounting. 5) Effects may be small or model-specific; multiple models and effect-size reporting mitigate this. 6) 'Better than natural language' may hold only on structured/symbolic tasks and fail on commonsense/factual tasks—this task-dependence is itself a key finding we characterize. 7) Cross-model transfer may be near-zero if dialects are idiosyncratic; a null transfer result still informs whether reasoning structure is shared or model-private.
